claim: Primary and secondary motor areas (M1 and M2) make functional synaptic connections in the globus pallidus (GP) in rats.
source: Here, we demonstrate in rats that primary and secondary motor areas (M1 and M2) make functional synaptic connections in the globus pallidus (GP), not usually thought of as an input site of the basal ganglia.
evidence: The claim is supported by both morphological observations showing cortical axons in the GP and electrophysiological recordings demonstrating functional synaptic responses.

claim: The density of axonal boutons from M1 in the GP was 47% of that in the subthalamic nucleus (STN).
source: Morphological observation revealed that the density of axonal boutons from motor cortices in the GP was 47% and 78% of that in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) from M1 and M2, respectively.
evidence: This is based on quantitative morphological measurements of axonal bouton density comparing GP and STN.

claim: The density of axonal boutons from M2 in the GP was 78% of that in the subthalamic nucleus (STN).
source: Morphological observation revealed that the density of axonal boutons from motor cortices in the GP was 47% and 78% of that in the subthalamic nucleus (STN) from M1 and M2, respectively.
evidence: This is based on quantitative morphological measurements of axonal bouton density comparing GP and STN.

claim: Cortical excitation of GP neurons was comparable to that of STN neurons in slice preparations.
source: Cortical excitation of GP neurons was comparable to that of STN neurons in slice preparations.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings showing similar optically evoked EPSC amplitudes in GP and STN neurons.

claim: FoxP2-expressing arkypallidal neurons were preferentially innervated by the motor cortex.
source: FoxP2-expressing arkypallidal neurons were preferentially innervated by the motor cortex.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from retrogradely labeled neurons combined with immunohistochemical identification of FoxP2 expression.

claim: The connection probability of cortico-pallidal innervation was higher for M2 than M1.
source: The connection probability of cortico-pallidal innervation was higher for M2 than M1.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that 151/248 neurons responded to M2 stimulation compared to 67/159 for M1 stimulation.

claim: Cortico-pallidal innervation is an additional excitatory input to the basal ganglia.
source: These results suggest that cortico-pallidal innervation is an additional excitatory input to the basal ganglia, and that it can affect behaviors via the cortex-basal ganglia-thalamus motor loop.
evidence: This is inferred from the morphological and electrophysiological evidence demonstrating functional cortical inputs to the GP.

claim: Cortico-pallidal innervation can affect behaviors via the cortex-basal ganglia-thalamus motor loop.
source: These results suggest that cortico-pallidal innervation is an additional excitatory input to the basal ganglia, and that it can affect behaviors via the cortex-basal ganglia-thalamus motor loop.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the anatomical and functional connectivity demonstrated in the study.

claim: Parallel loops of neural connections among the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and thalamus contribute to multiple aspects of behavior.
source: Parallel loops of neural connections among the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and thalamus contribute to multiple aspects of behavior (Alexander et al., 1986; Nambu, 2008; Wei and Wang, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The loop containing the motor cortex is crucial for appropriate motor control, action selection, and movement-related learning.
source: The loop containing the motor cortex is crucial for appropriate motor control, action selection, and movement-related learning.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge about motor cortex-basal ganglia loops.

claim: Dysfunction of the motor loop leads to movement disorders such as those seen in Parkinsonian disease.
source: Dysfunction of the motor loop leads to movement disorders such as those seen in Parkinsonian disease (Albin et al., 1989; DeLong, 1990; Middleton and Strick, 2002; Nambu, 2008; Nambu et al., 2000; Parent and Hazrati, 1995a; Redgrave et al., 2010; Wichmann and DeLong, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Cortical projections drive three pathways in the basal ganglia: the direct, the indirect, and the hyperdirect pathways.
source: Cortical projections drive three pathways in the basal ganglia: the direct, the indirect, and the hyperdirect pathways (Bolam et al., 2000; Smith et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge about basal ganglia circuitry, supported by citations.

claim: The hyperdirect pathway provides the fastest information flow among the three pathways.
source: The hyperdirect pathway involves direct cortical projections to the STN (Nambu et al., 2002), which provides the fastest information flow among the three pathways (Nambu et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Two types of GP neurons have been identified: one projects to the STN with or without projection to the striatum, while the other only projects to the striatum.
source: Recently, two types of GP neurons have been identified: one projects to the STN with or without projection to the striatum, while the other only projects to the striatum (Abdi et al., 2015; Dodson et al., 2015; Hernández et al., 2015; Mallet et al., 2012; Mastro et al., 2014), which has been implicated in the rewriting of neural circuitry involved in the GP.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The GP is now considered the hub of the basal ganglia, not simply a relay nucleus.
source: The GP is now considered the hub of the basal ganglia, not simply a relay nucleus (Hegeman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: In 1994, Naito and Kita reported cortical projections to the GP.
source: In 1994, Naito and Kita reported cortical projections to the GP, which raised the possibility of an additional neural pathway that can modulate the basal ganglia activities.
evidence: This is a historical reference to previous work.

claim: Cortical axons in the GP were dense in calbindin D-28k (CB)-negative regions.
source: For both M1 and M2 projections, cortical axons were dense in calbindin D-28k (CB) -negative [CB(-)] regions of the GP.
evidence: This is based on morphological observations using immunohistochemistry.

claim: The appearance of cortical axon varicosities in the GP was similar to those in the striatum and STN.
source: The appearance of cortical axon varicosities in the GP was similar to those in the striatum and STN (Figure 1A2 and C, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations shown in figures.

claim: Cortico-pallidal projections were exclusively ipsilateral.
source: Cortico-pallidal projections were exclusively ipsilateral (Figure 1D), implying that they did not stem from the intratelencephalon (IT) type of pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is based on anatomical tracing experiments showing no contralateral projections.

claim: Cortico-pallidal projections did not stem from the intratelencephalon (IT) type of pyramidal neurons.
source: Cortico-pallidal projections were exclusively ipsilateral (Figure 1D), implying that they did not stem from the intratelencephalon (IT) type of pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that projections are exclusively ipsilateral, as IT neurons typically project bilaterally.

claim: Cingulate area (Cg) and lateral orbitofrontal area (LO) also projected to the GP.
source: In addition, we found that cingulate area (Cg) and lateral orbitofrontal area (LO) also projected to the GP (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), although LO provided fewer axons than motor areas.
evidence: This is based on anatomical tracing experiments.

claim: LO provided fewer axons to the GP than motor areas.
source: In addition, we found that cingulate area (Cg) and lateral orbitofrontal area (LO) also projected to the GP (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2), although LO provided fewer axons than motor areas.
evidence: This is based on morphological observations comparing axon density.

claim: Cortical axons were differentially distributed in the GP, depending on the cortical area of origin.
source: Cortical axons were differentially distributed in the GP, depending on the cortical area of origin (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2; Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations showing different distribution patterns for different cortical areas.

claim: M1 and M2 axons were observed across the broad extent of the medio-lateral axis (range: M/L 2.4–4.2 mm from the midline).
source: M1 and M2 axons were observed across the broad extent of the medio-lateral axis (range: M/L 2.4–4.2 mm from the midline; see also Figure 2A, B and C), but relatively sparse in the medial and lateral portions in most cases (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations across multiple sections.

claim: LO axons were often located in the ventral part of the GP.
source: LO axons were often located in the ventral part of the GP, whereas Cg axons were dense in the more medial GP than M1/M2 axons.
evidence: This is based on morphological observations of axon distribution patterns.

claim: Cg axons were dense in the more medial GP than M1/M2 axons.
source: LO axons were often located in the ventral part of the GP, whereas Cg axons were dense in the more medial GP than M1/M2 axons.
evidence: This is based on morphological observations of axon distribution patterns.

claim: Varicosity density was greater in the striatum than in the GP or STN.
source: Varicosity density was apparently greater in the striatum than in the GP or STN (Figures 1A and 2B, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2, Table 1).
evidence: This is based on quantitative morphological measurements.

claim: The bouton density was significantly higher in the striatum than in the GP for both M1 and M2 projections.
source: Using this normalization, the bouton density was found to be significantly higher in the striatum than in the GP (Figure 2D; p=0.013, Kruskal Wallis test; p<10−7 for both M1 and M2 projections, Tukey-HSD test; not significant between M1 and M2, p=0.18)
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of quantitative morphological data.

claim: Normalized bouton densities in the GP were significantly different from those in the STN.
source: Normalized bouton densities in the GP were significantly different from those in the STN (Figure 2E; p=0.032, Kruskal-Wallis test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of quantitative morphological data.

claim: For M1 projections, STN-normalized bouton density was significantly smaller in the GP (0.496 ± 0.12) than in the STN.
source: For M1 projections, STN-normalized bouton density was significantly smaller in the GP (0.496 ± 0.12) than in the STN (p=0.0007, Tukey-HSD test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of quantitative morphological data.

claim: M2 had more boutons in the GP (0.778 ± 0.207) than M1.
source: Since M2 had more boutons in the GP (0.778 ± 0.207) than M1 (p=0.022), M2 bouton density did not significantly differ between the STN and the GP (p=0.09).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of quantitative morphological data.

claim: Stimulation with a brief light pulse elicited inward currents in GP neurons.
source: In voltage clamp mode at a holding potential of −60 mV, stimulation with a brief light pulse (5 ms, 470 nm) elicited inward currents in GP neurons (Figure 3B1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings with optogenetic stimulation.

claim: The response to photoactivation was stable over repetitive stimulation.
source: The response was stable over repetitive stimulation (10 pulses at 2–10 Hz; Figure 3B1).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings showing consistent responses.

claim: In current clamp mode, photoactivation elicited action potentials in GP neurons.
source: In current clamp mode, photoactivation elicited action potentials, although the action potential probability was affected by the spontaneous oscillation of the membrane potential (Figure 3B2).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings in current clamp mode.

claim: In half of the GP neurons, the rheobase was less than 30 pA.
source: In half of the GP neurons, the rheobase was less than 30 pA, and most GP neurons could emit an action potential with less than 100 pA of depolarization (N = 100 neurons; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements of rheobase current.

claim: Most GP neurons could emit an action potential with less than 100 pA of depolarization.
source: In half of the GP neurons, the rheobase was less than 30 pA, and most GP neurons could emit an action potential with less than 100 pA of depolarization (N = 100 neurons; Figure 3C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements of rheobase current.

claim: 67 out of 159 GP neurons exhibited inward photocurrents during M1 stimulation.
source: Not all GP neurons exhibited inward photocurrents, a total of 67/159 and 151/248 neurons did so during M1 and M2 stimulation, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from multiple neurons.

claim: 151 out of 248 GP neurons exhibited inward photocurrents during M2 stimulation.
source: Not all GP neurons exhibited inward photocurrents, a total of 67/159 and 151/248 neurons did so during M1 and M2 stimulation, respectively (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from multiple neurons.

claim: Neurons responding to M1 terminal stimulation tended to be located in the dorsal GP.
source: Neurons responding to M1 terminal stimulation tended to be located in the dorsal GP, whereas those responding to M2 terminal stimulation were clustered in the ventral GP (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on spatial mapping of recorded neurons.

claim: Neurons responding to M2 terminal stimulation were clustered in the ventral GP.
source: Neurons responding to M1 terminal stimulation tended to be located in the dorsal GP, whereas those responding to M2 terminal stimulation were clustered in the ventral GP (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is based on spatial mapping of recorded neurons.

claim: Bath application of TTX at 1 µM completely prevented inward currents.
source: Bath application of the sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX) at 1 µM completely prevented inward currents (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments.

claim: Additional application of 4AP at 1 mM recovered the currents to up to 60% of control on average.
source: Additional application of the potassium channel blocker 4-aminopyridine (4AP) at 1 mM recovered the currents to up to 60% of control on average (Figure 4A), indicating that the current was monosynaptic (Gradinaru et al., 2009; Shu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments demonstrating monosynaptic connectivity.

claim: The inward current was monosynaptic.
source: Additional application of the potassium channel blocker 4-aminopyridine (4AP) at 1 mM recovered the currents to up to 60% of control on average (Figure 4A), indicating that the current was monosynaptic (Gradinaru et al., 2009; Shu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the TTX/4AP experiment, which is a standard test for monosynaptic connections.

claim: A GABAA receptor antagonist (gabazine, 20 µM) did not block the current.
source: A GABAA receptor antagonist (gabazine, 20 µM) did not block the current (Figure 4A); conversely, glutamate receptor antagonists (CNQX, 10 μM and AP-5, 20 μM) almost completely abolished the current (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments.

claim: Glutamate receptor antagonists (CNQX, 10 μM and AP-5, 20 μM) almost completely abolished the current.
source: A GABAA receptor antagonist (gabazine, 20 µM) did not block the current (Figure 4A); conversely, glutamate receptor antagonists (CNQX, 10 μM and AP-5, 20 μM) almost completely abolished the current (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is based on pharmacological experiments.

claim: The inward current was mediated by glutamatergic excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs).
source: Thus, the inward current was mediated by glutamatergic excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs).
evidence: This is inferred from the pharmacological experiments showing blockade by glutamate receptor antagonists.

claim: The latency of current onset after the photic stimulus in GP neurons did not differ from that in STN neurons.
source: The latency (delay) of current onset after the photic stimulus in GP neurons did not differ from that in STN neurons (Figure 4B), which indicates that both EPSCs are directly elicited by cortical terminal activation.
evidence: This is based on comparative electrophysiological measurements.

claim: Both EPSCs in GP and STN are directly elicited by cortical terminal activation.
source: The latency (delay) of current onset after the photic stimulus in GP neurons did not differ from that in STN neurons (Figure 4B), which indicates that both EPSCs are directly elicited by cortical terminal activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar latencies observed in both neuron types.

claim: The 20–80% rise time and decay constant tended to be longer in GP neurons than in STN neurons.
source: The 20–80% rise time and decay constant tended to be longer in GP neurons than in STN neurons (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on comparative electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The motor cortex could innervate GP and STN using similar weights.
source: The normalized mean values were not significantly different from 1 (p>0.1, signed rank test), suggesting that the motor cortex could innervate GP and STN using similar weights, however, as the oEPSC amplitude largely varied across cells in both GP and STN neurons, the interpretation of this comparison must be made with caution.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of normalized oEPSC amplitudes, but the authors note caution in interpretation due to variability.

claim: GPSTN neurons usually showed spontaneous repetitive firing (~20 Hz).
source: GPSTN neurons usually showed spontaneous repetitive firing (~20 Hz; Table 1), whereas many GPCPu neurons were silent.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings of spontaneous activity.

claim: Many GPCPu neurons were silent.
source: GPSTN neurons usually showed spontaneous repetitive firing (~20 Hz; Table 1), whereas many GPCPu neurons were silent.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings of spontaneous activity.

claim: Firing frequencies induced by depolarizing current pulses were higher in GPSTN than in GPCPu neurons.
source: Firing frequencies induced by depolarizing current pulses were higher in GPSTN than in GPCPu neurons, and spike width was narrower in GPSTN neurons (Figure 5B; see Table 1 for other electrophysiological parameters and quantitative comparisons).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements comparing the two neuron types.

claim: Spike width was narrower in GPSTN neurons than in GPCPu neurons.
source: Firing frequencies induced by depolarizing current pulses were higher in GPSTN than in GPCPu neurons, and spike width was narrower in GPSTN neurons (Figure 5B; see Table 1 for other electrophysiological parameters and quantitative comparisons).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements comparing the two neuron types.

claim: GPCPu neurons (51/62) responded more frequently to optogenetic activation of motor cortical afferents than GPSTN neurons (53/126).
source: We discovered that GPCPu neurons (51/62) responded more frequently to opotogenetic activation of motor cortical afferents than GPSTN neurons (53/126), as shown in Figure 5C.
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from retrogradely labeled neurons.

claim: The oEPSC amplitude was larger in GPCPu neurons than in GPSTN neurons.
source: The oEPSC amplitude was also larger in GPCPu neurons (Figure 5D,E,F).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements comparing the two neuron types.

claim: The oEPSC amplitude was significantly larger in MSNs than in STN or GP neurons.
source: One-way ANOVA followed by post-hoc Tukey tests revealed that the oEPSC amplitude was significantly larger in MSNs than in STN or GP neurons (for all combinations of comparisons, p<9 × 10−7).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The oEPSC amplitude of STN neurons was not significantly different from that of GPSTN neurons.
source: The oEPSC amplitude of STN neurons was not significantly different from that of GPSTN (p=0.109) or GPCPu neurons (p=0.999).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: GPCPu neurons exhibited significantly greater oEPSC amplitudes than GPSTN neurons.
source: GPCPu neurons exhibited significantly greater amplitudes than GPSTN neurons (p=0.0021; Figure 5D).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The median of the rheobase current was 695 pA for MSNs.
source: Actually, the median of the rheobase current was 695 pA for MSNs (N = 10; range, 450–1415 pA), 55 pA for STN neurons (N = 30; range, 10–545 pA) and 30 pA for GP neurons (N = 100; range, 5–250 pA).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The median of the rheobase current was 55 pA for STN neurons.
source: Actually, the median of the rheobase current was 695 pA for MSNs (N = 10; range, 450–1415 pA), 55 pA for STN neurons (N = 30; range, 10–545 pA) and 30 pA for GP neurons (N = 100; range, 5–250 pA).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements.

claim: The median of the rheobase current was 30 pA for GP neurons.
source: Actually, the median of the rheobase current was 695 pA for MSNs (N = 10; range, 450–1415 pA), 55 pA for STN neurons (N = 30; range, 10–545 pA) and 30 pA for GP neurons (N = 100; range, 5–250 pA).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological measurements.

claim: GPCPu neurons were frequently innervated by either M1 (28/35) or M2 (23/27).
source: GPCPu neurons were frequently innervated by either M1 (28/35) or M2 (23/27).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from retrogradely labeled neurons.

claim: Only a small fraction of GPSTN neurons received M1 (17/51) or M2 (36/75) inputs.
source: In contrast, only a small fraction of GPSTN neurons received M1 (17/51) or M2 (36/75) inputs (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from retrogradely labeled neurons.

claim: The amplitude of M1-induced oEPSCs was significantly larger in the GPCPu neurons than in the GPSTN neurons.
source: The amplitude of M1-induced oEPSCs was significantly larger in the GPCPu neurons than in the GPSTN neurons (p=2.1 × 10−8, Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: The amplitude of M2-induced oEPSCs was significantly larger in the GPCPu neurons than in the GPSTN neurons.
source: This was also the case for M2-induced oEPSCs (p=0.00084).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Both motor areas preferentially innervated GPCPu neurons.
source: Therefore, both motor areas preferentially innervated GPCPu neurons, although GPSTN was more effectively innervated by M2 (Figure 5C F).
evidence: This is inferred from the higher connection probability and larger oEPSC amplitudes in GPCPu neurons.

claim: GPSTN was more effectively innervated by M2 than M1.
source: Therefore, both motor areas preferentially innervated GPCPu neurons, although GPSTN was more effectively innervated by M2 (Figure 5C F).
evidence: This is based on comparison of connection probabilities and oEPSC amplitudes.

claim: The mean oEPSC amplitude in GPSTN was larger with M2 stimulation than with M1 stimulation.
source: Indeed, the mean oEPSC amplitude in GPSTN was larger with M2 stimulation than with M1 stimulation (p=0.0028), but no significant difference between cortical sites was observed in GPCPu neurons (p=0.9595).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: GPCPu neurons frequently expressed FoxP2 or Lhx6, but not PV.
source: We confirmed that GPCPu neurons frequently expressed FoxP2 or Lhx6, but not PV (N = 659 GPCPu neurons in nine sections from three rats; Figure 6A), in agreement with previous studies in mice (Dodson et al., 2015; Hernández et al., 2015; Mastro et al., 2014; Mizutani et al., 2017), Long-Evans rats (Oh et al., 2017), and Sprague-Dawley rats (Abdi et al., 2015; Kita and Kita, 2001).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical analysis combined with retrograde labeling.

claim: The expression of FoxP2 and Lhx6 was almost mutually exclusive in GPCPu neurons.
source: The expression of FoxP2 and Lhx6 was almost mutually exclusive.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical analysis.

claim: Most PV(+) GPCPu neurons co-expressed Lhx6.
source: Most PV(+) GPCPu neurons co-expressed Lhx6.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical analysis.

claim: GPSTN neurons lacked expression of FoxP2 but expressed PV and/or Lhx6.
source: GPSTN neurons lacked expression of FoxP2 but expressed PV and/or Lhx6 (N = 727 GPSTN neurons in nine sections from three rats; Figure 6A).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical analysis combined with retrograde labeling.

claim: Only 14.7% of Lhx6-expressing GPCPu neurons co-expressed PV (49/333).
source: Only a small fraction (14.7%) of Lhx6-expressing neurons co-expressed PV (49/333) (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical analysis.

claim: GPSTN neurons comprised PV(+) and/or Lhx6(+) prototypic neurons.
source: Therefore, GPSTN neurons comprised PV(+) and/or Lhx6(+) prototypic neurons, whereas GPCPu neurons comprised arkypallidal neurons expressing FoxP2 and prototypic neurons expressing Lhx6 (Fujiyama et al., 2016; Mallet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular marker expression patterns and supported by citations.

claim: GPCPu neurons comprised arkypallidal neurons expressing FoxP2 and prototypic neurons expressing Lhx6.
source: Therefore, GPSTN neurons comprised PV(+) and/or Lhx6(+) prototypic neurons, whereas GPCPu neurons comprised arkypallidal neurons expressing FoxP2 and prototypic neurons expressing Lhx6 (Fujiyama et al., 2016; Mallet et al., 2012).
evidence: This is inferred from the molecular marker expression patterns and supported by citations.

claim: Lhx6 was expressed in most GPBi neurons (61/69).
source: Lhx6 was expressed in most GPBi neurons (61/69), PV less frequently (19/72), and FoxP2 rarely (2/85), as expected.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical analysis of double-retrogradely labeled neurons.

claim: PV was expressed less frequently in GPBi neurons (19/72).
source: Lhx6 was expressed in most GPBi neurons (61/69), PV less frequently (19/72), and FoxP2 rarely (2/85), as expected.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical analysis of double-retrogradely labeled neurons.

claim: FoxP2 was rarely expressed in GPBi neurons (2/85).
source: Lhx6 was expressed in most GPBi neurons (61/69), PV less frequently (19/72), and FoxP2 rarely (2/85), as expected.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical analysis of double-retrogradely labeled neurons.

claim: GPBi neurons that expressed PV co-expressed Lhx6 (5/6).
source: GPBi neurons that expressed PV co-expressed Lhx6, although the number of neurons examined was small (5/6).
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical analysis of double-retrogradely labeled neurons.

claim: GPBi neurons received cortical inputs (7/10 for M1 and 7/9 for M2).
source: We found that GPBi neurons received cortical inputs (7/10 for M1 and 7/9 for M2; N = 3 rats for each), although most of them exhibited oEPSCs with small amplitudes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from double-retrogradely labeled neurons.

claim: Most GPBi neurons exhibited oEPSCs with small amplitudes.
source: We found that GPBi neurons received cortical inputs (7/10 for M1 and 7/9 for M2; N = 3 rats for each), although most of them exhibited oEPSCs with small amplitudes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is based on electrophysiological recordings from double-retrogradely labeled neurons.

claim: The frequency distributions of oEPSC amplitudes significantly differed between GPBi and GPCPu neurons.
source: In fact, the frequency distributions of oEPSC amplitudes significantly differed between GPBi and GPCPu neurons (Figure 6D; p=2.2 × 10−16, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of electrophysiological data.

claim: Eight out of nine GPCPu neurons that exhibited oEPSCs expressed FoxP2.
source: We found that eight out of nine GPCPu neurons expressed FoxP2 (Figure 6E), suggesting that arkypallidal neurons are preferentially innervated by the motor cortex.
evidence: This is based on immunohistochemical analysis of recorded neurons.

claim: Arkypallidal neurons are preferentially innervated by the motor cortex.
source: We found that eight out of nine GPCPu neurons expressed FoxP2 (Figure 6E), suggesting that arkypallidal neurons are preferentially innervated by the motor cortex.
evidence: This is inferred from the high proportion of FoxP2-expressing neurons among those receiving cortical inputs.

claim: Cortico-pallidal projections exist in primates including humans.
source: A question that remains is whether cortico-pallidal projections exist in primates including humans, as has been suggested (Milardi et al., 2015; Smith and Wichmann, 2015).
evidence: This is a question raised based on previous suggestions in the literature.

claim: Pyramidal tract (PT) type pyramidal neurons are potential candidates for the origin of cortical neurons that provide axons in the GP.
source: Pyramidal tract (PT) type pyramidal neurons are potential candidates, because some collaterals were emitted from thick axon trunks passing the GP (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is speculated based on morphological observations.

claim: Layers 5 and 6 cortical neurons project to the GP in mice.
source: The most recent finding in mice suggested that layers 5 and 6 cortical neurons project to the GP (Abecassis et al., 2019), although it is not clear whether they project only to the GP.
evidence: This is based on a citation to recent literature.

claim: GPCPu neurons may increase firing more significantly than GPSTN neurons and be more in phase with cortical excitation.
source: Since GPCPu neurons are activated by direct M1 inputs, they may increase the firing more significantly than GPSTN neurons and be more in phase with cortical excitation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the preferential innervation of GPCPu neurons.

claim: Both MSNs and interneurons in the striatum are innervated by arkypallidal neurons.
source: With regard to synaptic targets of GPCPu neurons, Mallet et al. (2012) reported that both MSNs and interneurons in the striatum are innervated by arkypallidal neurons.
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous literature.

claim: Npas1(+) neurons synapse onto iMSNs and dMSNs in mice.
source: In mice, Npas1(+) neurons, which overlap with Lhx6(+) and FoxP2(+) GPCPu neurons, synapse onto iMSNs and dMSNs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about mouse basal ganglia circuitry.

claim: The average inhibitory postsynaptic current amplitude evoked by stimulation of axon terminals of Npas1(+) neurons is significantly larger in iMSNs than dMSNs.
source: The average inhibitory postsynaptic current amplitude evoked by stimulation of axon terminals of Npas1(+) neurons is significantly larger in iMSNs than dMSNs (Glajch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on a citation to previous literature.

claim: The M1 cortico-pallidal pathway may act as a delayed terminator of the hyperdirect pathway.
source: As the operation of this trisynaptic circuit should be slower than monosynaptic cortico-STN excitation (Figure 7), the M1 cortico-pallidal pathway may act as a delayed terminator of the hyperdirect pathway.
evidence: This is speculated based on the timing of different pathways.

claim: Striatal neurons receive contralateral cortical excitation as well as ipsilateral input.
source: In addition, it is noteworthy that striatal neurons receive contralateral cortical excitation as well as ipsilateral input (Wilson, 1986; Wilson, 1987), whereas the GP and STN receive only ipsilateral excitation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous literature and data from the current study.

claim: The GP and STN receive only ipsilateral excitation.
source: In addition, it is noteworthy that striatal neurons receive contralateral cortical excitation as well as ipsilateral input (Wilson, 1986; Wilson, 1987), whereas the GP and STN receive only ipsilateral excitation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is based on data from the current study showing exclusively ipsilateral projections.

claim: The hyperdirect pathway contributes to the cessation of ongoing actions.
source: Because the hyperdirect pathway contributes to the cessation of ongoing actions, the cortico-pallidal pathway may cancel this cessation signal.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the hyperdirect pathway.

claim: The cortico-pallidal pathway may cancel the cessation signal from the hyperdirect pathway.
source: Because the hyperdirect pathway contributes to the cessation of ongoing actions, the cortico-pallidal pathway may cancel this cessation signal.
evidence: This is speculated based on the potential interaction between pathways.

claim: M2 activation can relieve the motor dysfunction of Parkinson's disease in mice.
source: Recently, Magno et al. (2019) revealed that M2 activation can relieve the motor dysfunction of Parkinson's disease in mice.
evidence: This is based on a citation to recent literature.

claim: M2 contributes to the preparatory function.
source: M2 contributes to the preparatory function (Li et al., 2015; Svoboda and Li, 2018), as observed in primates (Wise, 1985), or increases its influence on other cortical areas during the preparatory phase (Makino et al., 2016; Makino et al., 2017).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous literature.

claim: GP neurons are suggested to compute action selection.
source: GP neurons are also suggested to compute action selection (Bogacz et al., 2016; Goldberg and Bergman, 2011), which likely relates to the preparation of movement, and the M2-pallidal pathway may therefore contribute.
evidence: This is based on citations to previous literature.

claim: M2 is involved in the integration of movement with sensory or internal information.
source: It has been also suggested that M2 is involved in the integration of movement with sensory or internal information (Barthas and Kwan, 2017; Saiki et al., 2014), including posture coding (Mimica et al., 2018).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous literature.
